Silicon Valley has a rule about Elon Musk and it fits on a single line: "Never bet against Elon Musk"

The rule traces back to Peter Thiel, the billionaire investor and Musk's former PayPal co-founder.

"I would never bet against Elon, in anything. That's hard rule number one."

Thiel's reasoning is simple. Musk keeps delivering what experts call mathematically and financially impossible. Mass-produced electric cars. Reusable orbital rockets.

The people who know him best stopped doubting him a long time ago.


Muskonomy (@muskonomy)

NEWS: Founders Fund holds SpaceX across nearly every fund it has raised and the lesson is to never bet against Elon, partner Trae Stephens says

Asked how much venture capital needs the SpaceX IPO, Stephens says the exposure spans the firm's venture and growth funds, with "a ton of exposure for LPs," both its earliest backers and its newest.

After 18 plus years holding the stock, his takeaway is blunt: "never bet against Elon. It's just a bad idea."

The listing now turns nearly two decades of conviction into liquidity, with the gains ready to roll into whatever comes next.

In 2008, Founders Fund invested in SpaceX.

At the time, the question wasn't whether SpaceX would dominate the launch market. The question was whether a rocket could reach orbit at all.

Trae Stephens, Founders Fund partner and co-founder of Anduril, says they first invested around Falcon 1's second flight. Three of the first four Falcon 1 launches had already failed.

They invested anyway.

At the time, Starlink was unimaginable. Data centers in space were science fiction. A $1.75 trillion valuation was not a thought anyone was having.

Today Stephens frames the SpaceX bet as "getting humanity to being a Kardashev Type II civilization."

One rocket in 2008. A civilization-scale outcome in 2026. Same holding.

This is what real conviction looks like. Not buying after the proof. Buying when the question was still whether it was physically possible.
